Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-154 — Failure execution contract

**Architecture ID:** CAT-ARCH-P4-EVIDENCE-154
**Title:** Failure runtime evidence card

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-220 — Completion execution contract

**Title:** Completion runtime evidence card

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Title:** Affiliate runtime evidence card
**Purpose:** Make the affiliate lifecycle executable, testable, observable, recoverable, and safe to evolve.
**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-242 — Request execution contract

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Title:** Content runtime evidence card
**Purpose:** Make the content lifecycle executable, testable, observable, recoverable, and safe to evolve.
**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-264 — Knowledge execution contract

**Title:** Knowledge runtime evidence card

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**Title:** Analytics runtime evidence card
**Purpose:** Make the analytics lifecycle executable, testable, observable, recoverable, and safe to evolve.
**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-286 — Decision execution contract

**Title:** Decision runtime evidence card
**Purpose:** Make the decision lifecycle executable, testable, observable, recoverable, and safe to evolve.

**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-352 — User execution contract

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. **AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**Primary Audience:** Human implementers, operators, reviewers, auditors, and Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or future AI coding agents.
**Reading Order:** Entry envelope; authority; components; timeline; durable facts; derived effects; failure; recovery; security; performance; evolution.

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

**Component Timeline:** Adapter accepts and normalizes; application coordinates; domain decides; repository commits; event adapter publishes; worker consumes; projection updates; policy filters reads; telemetry records every boundary.

**Event Timeline:** Command received, authorization decided, domain fact committed, integration event published, delivery attempted, handler outcome recorded, projection refreshed, and recovery event emitted when needed. Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.

**Implementation Contract:** Use the approved language and runtime. Use typed commands, queries, events, and errors. Propagate deadlines and cancellation. Make effects idempotent or compensatable. Pin dependencies. Version schemas. Provide health checks, metrics, traces, structured logs, migration plans, and rollback or forward-fix steps.

**AI Coding Contract:** The agent must inspect existing contracts before editing, state the authority and lifecycle transition, avoid unrelated rewrites, refuse to invent a missing permission, add negative and recovery tests, and report every assumption.

**AI Context Requirements:** Load `.ai/README.md`, root context, project overview, project rules, technology stack, this architecture part, owning domain context, ADRs, schemas, tests, deployment notes, security rules, and recovery runbooks. The context manifest records source order, scope, budget, deadline, and output contract.

**Validation Evidence:** Markdown and Mermaid structure; architecture IDs; dependency direction; runtime state transitions; execution timelines; journey maps; knowledge and context flow; cross-reference resolution; authorization, duplicate, timeout, partial-failure, replay, reconciliation, and recovery tests.

**Review Questions:** What is authoritative? Who owns each transition? What is the event? What happens twice? What happens when the dependency is absent? What can the operator stop? What is retained? What is deleted? How is scale bounded? How is success proved?

**Exception Rule:** Any deviation requires an owner, reason, risk, compensating control, expiry date, review trigger, and linked ADR. An unrecorded exception is a defect.

### P4-EVIDENCE-374 — Failure execution contract

**Title:** Failure runtime evidence card

**Architecture Decision Record:** The lifecycle is implemented as explicit state transitions behind owned ports. Authority remains in the owning domain. An external provider, cache, projection, agent, or operator screen cannot silently become the source of truth.

**Execution Story:** An attributable actor submits an intent. The gateway validates identity, tenant, schema, classification, deadline, and budget. Governance evaluates permission. The application invokes domain policy. The domain commits an authoritative fact or an explicit refusal. Events deliver work to idempotent handlers. Projections and notifications expose only permitted, freshness-labelled results.

**Execution Timeline:** T0 receive; T1 authenticate; T2 scope; T3 assemble context; T4 authorize; T5 validate invariants; T6 commit authority; T7 publish fact; T8 consume; T9 project; T10 notify; T11 measure; T12 close or recover.

Events include schema version, producer, tenant, correlation, causation, timestamp, and retention.

**Recovery Timeline:** Detect anomaly; classify transient, durable, unsafe, or unknown; stop unsafe effects; preserve evidence; retry or quarantine; repair or restore; replay or compensate; reconcile; verify invariants; communicate; record learning.

**Failure Timeline:** Failure may occur at ingress, policy, domain, storage, event publication, delivery, external API, projection, notification, or operator action. Each failure has a bounded response and a terminal observable state.

**Future Evolution:** In 2026 keep the modular boundary and evidence cheap to operate. By 2030 support larger tenant and event volume without losing ownership. By 2035 preserve identifiers, schemas, authority, sovereignty, and recovery while replacing runtimes and providers.

**Performance Contract:** Define request latency class, event lag, throughput, concurrency, payload limits, storage growth, provider rate limits, cache freshness, cost budget, and recovery rate. Alert on SLO burn and saturation before correctness is threatened.

**Security Contract:** Require authenticated identity, explicit tenant, least privilege, policy version, data classification, approval where required, audit receipt, redaction, secret hygiene, and tenant-isolation tests. Refusal is safer than ambiguous execution.

**Repository Mapping:** Domain state and invariants belong in the owning context; application orchestration belongs in its use-case module; adapters, migrations, schemas, dashboards, and runbooks belong in approved infrastructure paths; tests remain close to the contract.
